Keywords: i knew you

outputs.L1: I knew you before you had a mother, when you were newtlike, swimming—a horrible brain in water. outputs.L2:
I recognized you before any mother existed for you, back when you were like a small amphibian, drifting through liquid—an awful mind suspended in water. I recognized you when every nerve and link in you referred only back to you, before you possessed any past to cling to, little barnacle; before metal could nourish you, before there was any vessel to carry you onward, while you remained fixed in one spot, moving only against the riddle of being.

I recognized you when you were nothing but sight and a mixed drink, as empty as the sky inside a thought; a root with neither earth nor placenta. You had not yet been reddened by injury or shocked into pain. One dreadful eye stood open in the middle of your skull, facing the dark, revolving, while the stars winked like a cat.

Before milk from the breast was known to us, we floated together in the final thin stream of champagne. We shared the darkness of the cupboard, the parasite sealing itself over our thumbprint; we were blurred marks inside a yellow book. My son, we were oak before speech, whole and uncarved; we had courage before we had memory.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on knowing her son even before his birth, imagining him in the earliest stage of existence, when he was still formless, “newtlike,” and suspended in water. This image presents the unborn child as something both human and not yet fully human, a small primitive life developing in the hidden world of the womb. He is pictured as existing before ordinary life began, before memory, history, pain, or any need to depend on the outside world.

The poem evokes a shared prenatal existence defined by darkness, mystery, and a deep, instinctive awareness. In this space, mother and child are connected before language, before identity, and before the child has any separate experience of the world. The speaker’s imagery makes this early state feel both strange and intimate. References to eyes, roots, stars, and the womb suggest a life that is at once biological, cosmic, and deeply personal.

Through these images, the poem presents pregnancy as a mysterious beginning shared by mother and child. The son’s earliest existence is not described simply as physical development, but as a brave, wordless state of becoming. Before he had memories, a name, or a clear identity of his own, he and his mother were joined in a hidden, primal world. The poem ultimately suggests that their bond began before birth, in a dark and silent place where life was just beginning to take shape.
outputs.L4:
The poem reflects on the mysterious state of existence before birth, imagining prenatal life as something fluid, bodily, and only partly human. It addresses a “son” who is not yet fully formed as an individual, but instead seems to exist as a primitive consciousness suspended in a world before memory, language, and ordinary identity. Through surreal images of the body, water, darkness, and origin, the poem presents the unborn child as both intimate and strange: close to the speaker, yet also alien, ancient, and unknowable.

Rather than describing infancy in a sentimental way, the poem reaches further back, into a time before pain, history, and self-awareness. It suggests that before a person becomes shaped by suffering, experience, and dependency, there is another kind of being: instinctive, innocent, and strangely courageous. The “son” is imagined as living in a state where fear has not yet fully entered, where identity has not yet separated itself from the body that carries it. This makes prenatal existence seem almost mythic, as though the child belongs not only to the speaker but also to a deeper, older world of beginnings.

The poem’s imagery creates a sense of both tenderness and unease. The unborn child is vulnerable and dependent, but also powerful in his raw persistence. He exists in darkness, in fluid, in a space that is protective but also uncanny. The speaker appears to look back toward this condition with wonder, trying to understand what life was before consciousness and memory began. In doing so, the poem turns the womb into a symbolic place of origin, where human life is not yet separate from the strange physical processes that create it.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that the earliest form of existence is shared, bodily, and mysterious. Before the son becomes a distinct person with his own memories and wounds, he is part of a more primal intimacy. This state is innocent, but not simple; it is brave, but not fully aware of itself. By presenting prenatal life in surreal and unsettling terms, the poem makes birth and identity feel less like clear beginnings and more like transformations out of a hidden, ancient, and deeply intimate world.
outputs.L5:
**I Knew You**

I knew you before I understood what knowing someone truly meant.

Not in the way people know a name, a favorite song, or the small details collected through time. I knew you in the quiet spaces between words, in the way your silence still said something, in the way your presence could change the feeling of an entire room.

I knew you in moments that seemed ordinary then but became unforgettable later. The way you laughed when you were trying not to. The way your eyes softened when you listened. The way you carried both strength and sadness like they had learned to live together inside you.

Maybe I didn’t know everything. Maybe there were parts of you hidden even from yourself. But I knew enough to recognize you—not just your face, not just your voice, but the feeling of you.

And even now, after distance, after time, after everything we never said, a part of me still thinks:

I knew you.

And somehow, I always will.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in lowercase from the perspective of a parent addressing an unborn son, full of embryonic imagery, strange metaphors, and a haunting, intimate tone.
counterfactuals.output:
my son, my small weather sealed in the red room, you turn like a thought before it learns language. i hear you in the dark aquarium of your mother, a moon with no sky, a fist opening and closing around nothing, practicing hunger, practicing prayer.

you are not yet born, and already you have the privacy of a star. already you drift farther from me than any man i have loved or buried. i speak to the door of your mother’s body and imagine you listening with the soft shells of your becoming, your ears like pale seeds, your spine a ladder built by ghosts.

outside, the trees go on being trees, foolish and vertical. the kettle screams. dust gathers on the windowsill with the patience of old snow. but inside, inside you are assembling yourself from blueprints of salt and lightning. your heart knocks in its tiny house. your blood rehearses the red road. your bones, those white rumors, begin their slow argument with the dark.

i want to tell you the world is gentle, but the world has teeth under its tongue. i want to promise you my hands will always be larger than fear, but i have seen fear wear my face in the mirror. still, i am here, bending toward you like a burned candle, whispering through skin and water: come when you must, little comet, little drowned king, little animal made of milk and thunder.

your mother sleeps, and you float beneath her dreams, a secret with eyelashes. perhaps you are dreaming too. perhaps you dream of fields before grass, of birds before wings, of my voice as a low tide pulling at the walls of your first ocean. perhaps you think i am the monster outside the cave. perhaps i am.

forgive me. already i have given you a world with knives in the drawer, clocks on the wall, names waiting like collars. already i have imagined your face so many times i have made a thousand strangers out of you. one has my mouth. one has her eyes. one is faceless and luminous, a lantern wrapped in blood.

sleep there, if sleep is what you do. grow your small storms. knit your fingers from the thread of ancestors. drink the dark. one day the room will split open and the air will enter you like a verdict. one day you will cry, and i will answer, and neither of us will know whether we are greeting each other or mourning the place you left behind.

until then, my son, remain unbroken in your warm eclipse. i will stand beside the invisible river, listening for your oar.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, experimental monologue that begins “i knew you before you had a mother” and explores pre-birth memory, water, anatomy, and ancestry in a disturbing lyrical style.
counterfactuals.output:
i knew you before you had a mother, before the word mother grew a mouth and fastened itself to the warm animal of her body, before the room of her pelvis learned your weather, before milk rehearsed its white ghost in the dark ducts, before anyone counted fingers like small prophecies and declared you possible.

You were a salt idea then. A tremor in the old water.

Do not ask me how memory survives without a skull. It does. It clings to minerals. It nests in cartilage before cartilage is named. It floats in the amniotic hush with its blind face turned upward, listening to the machinery of blood. You remember without thinking. You remember as kelp remembers the moon, as teeth remember the jaw of some vanished fish, as the spine remembers the first lightning that taught it to arch.

There was water before there was you, and the water was crowded.

Grandmothers swam there with their hair unpinned and their bones full of war. Great-grandfathers opened and closed their mouths like drowned bells. Aunts unborn, brothers miscarried, children folded back into the red library of the body—all of them pressed their palms against the membrane and whispered instructions. Grow here. Harden there. Divide. Become more than a bruise. Become a door that screams when opened.

Your first house was not a house but a wound that loved you. Its walls pulsed. Its ceiling wept. Its floor was nowhere. You hung by your hunger, tethered to a red rope, fed on a woman’s hidden tides. Her heart was the drum in the next room, enormous, ignorant, faithful. Her lungs were two wet wings beating above you. Her intestines muttered their long ancestral prayers. You slept beneath the liver’s dark continent, beneath the ribs’ pale cage, beneath the sternum’s locked gate, and every organ was a relative speaking in a dialect of squeeze and flood.

I was there too.

Not as a face. Not as a name. Names came later, those little coffins for the infinite. I was the pressure behind your forming eyes. I was the black shine in the seed. I was the old witness curled in the spiral of the ear, teaching you the ocean before you ever saw light. I licked the vernix from your shoulders in the future. I counted the translucent ladders of your ribs before skin made you secret. I knew the blue map of your veins when they were only rumors.

You were not innocent. Nothing that comes from blood is innocent.

Inside you, a museum opened. In one room: a famine, gnawing its own knuckles. In another: a woman biting cloth so the soldiers would not hear her give birth. In another: a field stitched with bones and wheat. In another: the first ancestor who crawled from the water and missed it forever. Each of them left something in you—an eyelid, a fear of knives, the shape of a molar, the habit of flinching when love raises its hand too quickly. You did not inherit stories. You inherited instructions for surviving stories.

Listen: the body is not singular. The body is a parliament of ghosts.

Your kneecaps were argued over by the dead. Your tongue was voted into being by women who swallowed their own names. Your hands carry the memory of tools, throats, infants, doors barred from the inside. Your blood is a river full of old weather. It does not begin in you. It passes through you with its silt of plague and lullaby, with its drowned horses, its bridal veils, its rusted keys.

Before birth, you had gills of attention. You drank sound through your skin. You learned grief as vibration: the mother crying without tears, the mother laughing too hard, the mother’s pulse bolting like a horse in a burning stable. You knew hunger before mouth. You knew fear before thought. You knew love as chemistry, as sugar crossing a border, as warmth arriving unasked through a cord that could have strangled you and did not.

Sometimes I think birth is only water remembering fire.

The rupture, the gush, the red animal door. The hands. The glare. The first air entering like glass. The body suddenly separate and therefore doomed. They lifted you from the flood and you became an I. Terrible little pronoun. Blade of a word. You opened your mouth and the ancestors flew in, black birds, one after another, roosting in the rafters of your chest.

And still, some nights, you hear it: the old aquarium, the maternal thunder, the soft collapse of fluid around your almost-body. You dream of being boneless and known. You dream of returning through the navel, unmaking the scar, swimming backward past the heart, past the egg, past the first division, past the pale hand of God or accident or hunger—back to the water where no one has a mother because everyone is mother, because the sea has one enormous womb and it is full of teeth, full of songs, full of children who remember us before we arrive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short piece of poetic prose about knowing someone before they existed, using images of embryos, eyes, milk, champagne, closets, books, and trees; make it eerie and beautiful.
counterfactuals.output:
I knew you before you had a name, before your eyes floated up from the dark like two small moons under water. You were no larger than an embryo of light, folded in the red hush, dreaming your way toward skin.

In the closet, the dresses breathed without bodies inside them. On the shelves, books opened themselves to pages about trees, their black branches climbing into sentences. I left out bowls of milk for what had not yet arrived, and glasses of champagne for what had already been lost.

Even then, I could hear you rustling in the roots. Even then, the forest leaned close, as if every leaf had seen your face before it was made.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output: my child, i knew you before the red door of birth swung open, before memory grew its moldy teeth and bit the world into names; i knew you when you were a blue whisper curled in the marrow of my sleep, a small moon stitched from milk, flies, and thunder, drifting through the black broth where unborn things learn to hum; i carried your shadow before i carried your body, saw your face floating in the eye of a goat, in the yolk of a fever, in the wet wallpaper peeling from heaven’s mouth; you were already calling to me from under the floorboards of time, tapping with your tiny bones, asking to be made of hunger and light; and when you arrived, slick as a drowned star, screaming with the voice of every animal ever buried, i did not meet you, no, i remembered you, my little omen, my sweet wound, my ancient stranger wrapped in skin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of avant-garde confessional poetry: a parent speaks to a son about the primordial time before identity, using biological, nautical, and surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Son,

before your name  
was a small boat nailed to your forehead,  
before I learned to call myself  
the harbor,

we were weather  
inside weather.

No mother yet.  
No child.  
Only the blind algebra of cells  
dividing their dark bread,  
only salt rehearsing the sea  
in the red cave of the body.

I confess:  
I did not love you first as you.  
I loved the pulse without a face,  
the rumor in the blood,  
the little moon-fish turning  
in its private ocean.

You were not innocent then—  
innocence requires a mirror.  
You were older than innocence,  
older than the word son,  
a pre-human lantern  
swinging from the mast of my ribs.

At night I heard you  
like a shell hears catastrophe:  
not sound, exactly,  
but the future dragging its anchor  
across the floor of me.

My body became  
a ship with no country.  
My spine, a wet rope.  
My heart, a deckhand  
throwing red buckets overboard.  
And you—  
you slept in the hold  
among starfish, chromosomes,  
small blue explosions.

Forgive me  
for making a world  
out of hunger and bone.

Forgive the first border: skin.  
Forgive the first exile: birth.  
Forgive the mouth  
for inventing names  
where once there was only  
warmth, current,  
the luminous mud of becoming.

Before identity,  
we were not two.  
We were a tide thinking itself.  
We were a question  
with gills.  
We were the sea  
dreaming of lungs.

And then you arrived—  
red, furious,  
covered in the proof  
that paradise is viscous.

I held you  
and the universe became grammatical:  
I, you, mine,  
loss.

Still, some nights,  
when sleep unbuttons the room,  
I feel us return—  
past father, past son,  
past the cruel lighthouse of the self—

to that first black water  
where no one is forgiven  
because no one  
has yet been named.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
